TRADING STOCK DEFICIT: The stated deficit of R22 150 was calculated WITHOUT considering the following: M Vrede (a debtor) returned merchandise of R31 200 (at selling price) on 28 February 2025 — this was NOT recorded. The returned goods were placed back into stock. Ebony Ltd maintains a consistent mark-up of 60% on cost.

subQuestions.memoText:
EBONY LTD — STATEMENT OF COMPREHENSIVE INCOME (Year ended 28 February 2025)

• Why subtract R31 200: M Vrede's return was unrecorded — it reduces sales.

Other income: R225 250 ✓
• Service fee income: R174 580 (given)

  Teaching point: When provision DECREASES, the difference is credited to income, not deducted from expenses.
• Rent income: 72 960 ÷ 12 = R6 080/month. Rented from 1 July 2024 → 8 months in the year. Income for year = 6 080 × 8 = R48 640 ✓✓
  OR: 72 960 − (6 080 × 4 months advance) = 72 960 − 24 320 = R48 640
  The 4 months advance (March–June 2025) is income received in advance (liability), NOT income for this year.

Gross operating income: 4 552 500 + 225 250 = R4 777 750 ✓

Operating expenses: R(3 307 800) ✓
• Salaries and wages: R763 000 (given)
• Depreciation: R285 860 (given)
• Audit fees: 75 168 + 18 792 (accrued) = R93 960 ✓✓
• Directors' fees: R1 452 330 ✓
  Working: The March 2025 fees (paid in advance) must be EXCLUDED from this year's expense.
  Each existing director's monthly fee = 1 595 385 ÷ 13 months ÷ 2... actually:
  Monthly fee per existing director = R49 500 (derived from memo: 49 500 + 49 500 + 44 055 = 143 055 for March)
  Third director monthly fee = 49 500 − 5 445 = R44 055 ✓

  (Remove the March 2025 fees that were pre-paid: 49 500 × 2 + 44 055 = 143 055)

• Sundry expenses: R710 000 ✓

Operating profit: 4 777 750 − 3 307 800 = R1 469 950 ✓

Interest income: R59 450 ✓ (balancing figure — derived last)

  Less capital repayment = 126 600

  OR: 1 326 000 − 397 800 = R928 200
  Teaching: Tax = 30% → after-tax = 70% → NPAT = 397 800 ÷ 30 × 70 = 928 200

PENALTIES: −1 for each foreign item (SFP items placed in income statement), max −2. −1 for poor presentation, max −1.

subQuestions.label: 2.1(i)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the carrying value of BUILDINGS on 1 March 2024.

INFORMATION D — Fixed Asset Note (extract) for PREMIER LTD:

FIXED ASSETS         | BUILDINGS (R)  | VEHICLES (R) | EQUIPMENT (R)
Carrying value 1 Mar 2024 | (i) = ?   | 1 473 000   | 1 450 000
Cost               |               | 3 223 000   | 2 630 000
Accum. depreciation|      0        | (1 750 000) | (1 180 000)
Movements:         |               |             |
Additions          | 7 909 600     |      0      | 320 000
Disposals          |      0        |    (ii)     |      0
Depreciation       |      0        |             |    (iii)
Carrying value 28 Feb 2025 | 15 479 600 |          |           |
Accum. depreciation|      0        |             |

Additional information on fixed assets:
• Extensions to the buildings were completed during the financial year.
• An old vehicle was sold at CARRYING VALUE on 30 September 2024. Cost: R510 000; accumulated depreciation on 1 March 2024: R330 000.
• Vehicles are depreciated at 20% p.a. on carrying value (diminishing balance).

subQuestions.memoText:
Carrying value of buildings on 1 March 2024:

Working: Closing carrying value − Additions = Opening carrying value
15 479 600 − 7 909 600 = R7 570 000 ✓✓

Teaching point: Buildings have zero depreciation (land/buildings not depreciated) and no disposals, so the only movement is the addition of R7 909 600. Work backwards from the known closing value.

subQuestions.label: 2.1(ii)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the disposal of the vehicle at carrying value (the figure that would appear under 'Disposals' in the Vehicles column of the Fixed Asset Note).

Use the Fixed Asset Note and additional information from 2.1(i) above:
• Vehicle sold at carrying value on 30 September 2024.
• Cost price: R510 000
• Accumulated depreciation on 1 March 2024: R330 000
• Depreciation rate: 20% p.a. on carrying value (diminishing balance method)
subQuestions.memoText:
Disposal of vehicle at carrying value:

Step 1 — Carrying value on 1 March 2024:
R510 000 − R330 000 = R180 000 ✓✓

Step 2 — Depreciation for period 1 March 2024 to 30 September 2024 (7 months):
R180 000 × 20% × 7/12 = R21 000 ✓✓

Step 3 — Carrying value at date of disposal (30 September 2024):
R510 000 − R330 000 − R21 000 = R159 000 ✓

Answer: R159 000 (disposal at carrying value)

Alternative working: 510 000 − 351 000 (total accumulated depreciation at disposal) = R159 000 ✓

Teaching points:
• Sold AT carrying value means NO profit or loss on disposal.
• The disposal figure in the fixed asset note = carrying value AT the date of sale (not at year-start).
• You must calculate the partial-year depreciation BEFORE determining the disposal value.
• The vehicle column depreciation in the note covers ONLY the remaining vehicles (not the disposed one).
subQuestions.topic: Fixed Assets - Disposal at Carrying Value

subQuestions.label: 2.1(iii)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the TOTAL depreciation on equipment for the year ended 28 February 2025.

Use the Fixed Asset Note from 2.1(i) above:
• OLD equipment (in use from 1 March 2024): cost R2 630 000
• NEW equipment purchased on 1 December 2024: cost R320 000
• Depreciation rate: 15% p.a. on COST (straight-line method)
subQuestions.memoText:
Total depreciation on equipment:

OLD equipment (full year — 12 months):
R2 630 000 × 15% × 12/12 = R394 500 ✓✓

NEW equipment (purchased 1 December 2024 — 3 months: Dec, Jan, Feb):
R320 000 × 15% × 3/12 = R12 000 ✓✓

Total depreciation on equipment:
R394 500 + R12 000 = R406 500 ✓

Answer: R406 500

NOTE: Do NOT award marks if anything else is added to R320 000 or R2 630 000 as stand-alone figures.

Teaching point: Equipment uses cost (straight-line), not carrying value. Pro-rate new equipment from purchase date. Old equipment runs the full 12 months.

subQuestions.label: 2.2 (Taxation paid)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the TAXATION PAID to SARS during the year ended 28 February 2025 for Premier Ltd.

INFORMATION B — Extract from Statement of Financial Position:
                        28 Feb 2025    29 Feb 2024
SARS: Income tax (asset)   R220 000          R0
SARS: Income tax (liability)    R0         R148 000

INFORMATION A — Income tax per Income Statement:
Income tax for the year: R1 736 000
subQuestions.memoText:
Taxation paid:

Using the SARS: Income tax ledger account (T-account) approach:

Opening balance (liability, i.e., owed to SARS): R148 000 ✓
+ Current year income tax expense: R1 736 000 ✓
+ Closing balance (asset, i.e., overpaid / SARS owes us): R220 000 ✓
= Total tax paid: 148 000 + 1 736 000 + 220 000 = R2 104 000 ✓

Answer: R2 104 000

Alternative: −148 000 − 1 736 000 − 220 000 = (R2 104 000) [signs reversed; accept with brackets]

Teaching point:
• When opening balance is a LIABILITY (we owed SARS), it means we PAID that too.
• When closing balance is an ASSET (SARS owes us), it means we OVERPAID — add to total paid.
• Formula: Tax paid = Opening liability + Current year tax + Closing asset
  (or: Opening liability + Current year tax − Closing liability)
Ignore brackets in workings.

subQuestions.label: 2.2 (Dividends paid)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate the DIVIDENDS PAID during the year ended 28 February 2025 for Premier Ltd.

INFORMATION B — Extract from Statement of Financial Position:
                            28 Feb 2025    29 Feb 2024
Shareholders for dividends   R1 400 000     R840 000

INFORMATION C — Shares and dividends:
• 3 000 000 shares in issue on 1 March 2024.
• 1 050 000 new shares issued on 30 June 2024 at R6 300 000.
• Interim dividend of 32 cents per share paid on 31 August 2024.
• 50 000 shares repurchased on 31 October 2024.
• Final dividend declared on 28 February 2025.
subQuestions.memoText:
Dividends paid:

Shares in issue on 31 August 2024 (when interim dividend paid):
3 000 000 + 1 050 000 = 4 050 000 shares ✓

Interim dividend declared/paid: 4 050 000 × 32c = R1 296 000 ✓✓

Using Shareholders for Dividends ledger approach:
Opening balance (SFD): R840 000 ✓
+ Interim dividends: R1 296 000 ✓✓
= Available to pay: R2 136 000
− Closing balance (SFD): R1 400 000
= Dividends paid during year: R840 000 + R1 296 000 = R2 136 000 ✓

Answer: R2 136 000

Alternative: 840 000 + [2 696 000 − 1 400 000] = 840 000 + 1 296 000 = R2 136 000

Teaching point:
• Dividends PAID = opening SFD balance (last year's final div paid this year) + interim dividends paid this year.
• The CLOSING SFD balance (R1 400 000) is this year's FINAL dividend — declared but not yet paid, so it stays in the SFP.

subQuestions.questionText:
According to the Fixed Asset Note, Premier Ltd completed extensions to the building for R7 909 600 during the financial year.

(a) Name TWO major sources of funding for the extensions (over R2 000 000 each), with figures.
(b) For EACH source, state ONE different way the cash flow will be NEGATIVELY affected in the future.

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose the correct word from the brackets. Write only the word.

Effective control of expenses in the business is a reflection of (risk / profitability).
subQuestions.memoText:
Profitability ✓

Teaching: Controlling operating expenses well (keeping them low relative to sales) directly improves the net profit margin — this is a measure of profitability, not risk.

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose the correct word from the brackets. Write only the word.

When a company is liquidated, the shareholders' liability will be (limited / unlimited), as they will not be held responsible for company debts.
subQuestions.memoText:
Limited ✓

NOTE: No abbreviations accepted (e.g. 'Ltd' is not acceptable).

Teaching: In a company (unlike a sole trader or partnership), shareholders enjoy LIMITED LIABILITY — they can only lose the amount they invested in shares. They are NOT personally liable for the company's debts.

subQuestions.questionText:
Choose the correct word from the brackets. Write only the word.

(Solvency / Liquidity) is the ability of the business to pay off ALL its debts using existing assets.
subQuestions.memoText:
Solvency ✓

Teaching:
• SOLVENCY = ability to pay ALL debts (both short-term and long-term) using ALL assets. It is a long-term concept measured by the solvency ratio (Total Assets : Total Liabilities).
• LIQUIDITY = ability to pay SHORT-TERM debts using current assets. It is a short-term concept measured by the current ratio and acid-test ratio.

subQuestions.questionText:
LIQUIDITY — Venus Ltd:

The liquidity position of the company has IMPROVED. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures to support this statement.

INFORMATION A — Financial indicators for Venus Ltd:
                              28 Feb 2025    29 Feb 2024
Current ratio                   1.6 : 1        0.3 : 1
Acid-test ratio                 0.8 : 1        0.1 : 1
Debtors' collection period      36 days        43 days
Creditors' payment period       63 days        63 days
subQuestions.memoText:
TWO financial indicators showing improved liquidity (2 marks each: 1 for indicator + figures, 1 for trend explanation):

Option 1: Current ratio IMPROVED/INCREASED from 0.3 : 1 to 1.6 : 1 (by 1.3 : 1) ✓✓
Option 2: Acid-test ratio IMPROVED/INCREASED from 0.1 : 1 to 0.8 : 1 (by 0.7 : 1) ✓✓
Option 3: Debtors' collection period IMPROVED/DECREASED from 43 days to 36 days (by 7 days) ✓✓

Do NOT accept creditors' payment period (unchanged at 63 days and not a liquidity measure).

Teaching: For liquidity, current ratio and acid-test ratios must INCREASE. Debtors collecting faster (fewer days) improves cash flow and thus liquidity.

subQuestions.label: 3.3 (Dividend pay-out rate)
subQuestions.questionText:
DIVIDEND PAY-OUT POLICY — Venus Ltd:

Calculate the dividend pay-out rate for the year ended 28 February 2025.

INFORMATION A — Financial indicators:
• Earnings per share (28 Feb 2025): 51 cents
• Dividends per share (28 Feb 2025): 55 cents
• Dividend pay-out rate (29 Feb 2024): 60.3%
subQuestions.memoText:
Dividend pay-out rate:

Formula: Dividends per share ÷ Earnings per share × 100
= 55c ÷ 51c × 100 ✓
= 107.8% ✓✓

Answer: 107.8%

Do NOT accept 1.07 or 107% (must show one decimal).

Teaching: A dividend pay-out rate ABOVE 100% means the company paid MORE in dividends than it earned — it is paying from retained income/reserves. This is unsustainable long-term but may reflect a once-off decision to reward shareholders from accumulated reserves.

subQuestions.label: 3.3 (Reason for policy change)
subQuestions.questionText:
DIVIDEND PAY-OUT POLICY — Venus Ltd:

The dividend pay-out rate CHANGED from 60.3% (29 Feb 2024) to 107.8% (28 Feb 2025). Explain why the directors decided to change the policy. Give ONE reason.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid reason ✓✓ (2 marks for a well-explained point; 1 mark for a partial/incomplete response):

• The company wants to keep shareholders happy / increase shareholder satisfaction.
• They are trying to INFLUENCE the MARKET PRICE of shares by increasing dividends (share price was declining).
• Equalising dividends over several years (smoothing).
• The company is NOT planning for future expansions — choosing to distribute instead.
• The company had sufficient accumulated reserves from previous years to support the higher dividend.

Teaching: Companies sometimes pay dividends above earnings when:
(a) They want to signal confidence to the market.
(b) They have excess retained earnings.
(c) They want to maintain a stable/progressive dividend policy.

subQuestions.label: 3.4 (New shares purchased by Denzel)
subQuestions.questionText:
% SHAREHOLDING AND REPURCHASE DECISION-MAKING — Venus Ltd:

Calculate the number of NEW shares that Denzel Crous purchased on 31 July 2024.

INFORMATION C — Shares of Venus Ltd:
• In issue on 29 February 2024: 900 000
• In issue on 28 February 2025: 950 000
• New shares issued on 31 July 2024 at R10.50 each: 125 000
• Repurchased on 1 December 2024 at R12.00 each: 75 000

INFORMATION D — Shareholding of Denzel Crous:

• Number of shares owned on 28 February 2025: 494 000
subQuestions.memoText:
Number of new shares Denzel purchased on 31 July 2024:

Step 1 — Denzel's shares on 29 February 2024:
900 000 × 45% = 405 000 shares ✓

Step 2 — New shares purchased:
494 000 (closing) − 405 000 (opening) = 89 000 shares ✓

Answer: 89 000 shares ✓

Alternative working: 495 000 − 456 000 + 50 000 = 89 000 ✓✓✓
(or: 125 000 − 75 000 = 50 000 net new shares; working differently)

NOTE: Do NOT award marks for operations done to stand-alone figures.

Teaching: Total shares at year-end = 900 000 + 125 000 − 75 000 = 950 000 ✓. Denzel did not sell any shares — his increase of 89 000 came from the new issue on 31 July 2024.

subQuestions.label: 3.4 (Denzel's % shareholding)
subQuestions.questionText:
Calculate Denzel's % shareholding in Venus Ltd on 28 February 2025.

INFORMATION C & D:
• Total shares in issue on 28 February 2025: 950 000
• Denzel's shares on 28 February 2025: 494 000

Denzel's % shareholding:

= 494 000 ÷ 950 000 × 100 ✓

subQuestions.label: 3.4 (Auditor concern)
subQuestions.questionText:
The independent auditor discovered that Denzel had made the decision to repurchase shares from the estate of a deceased relative on 1 December 2024 WITHOUT informing the board of directors.

Why should the independent auditor be concerned about this? Give ONE reason.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid reason ✓✓ (2 marks for a well-explained point; 1 mark for a partial/incomplete response):

• UNETHICAL: Denzel is taking advantage of his position as the majority shareholder — this creates a potential conflict of interest.
• NEPOTISM: Denzel favoured his relative's estate by paying R12 per share (above the market price of R10 per share).
• NOT PROCEDURAL: One person (the CFO) cannot unilaterally determine share buy-back prices — this requires board approval.
• SHAREHOLDERS may lodge a dispute as this action could be a BREACH of the company's policies and the Companies Act.
• The decision was NOT fair and transparent.

subQuestions.label: 3.5 (Should not borrow more)
subQuestions.questionText:
GEARING AND RISK — Venus Ltd:

The directors want to expand by opening more branches. Explain why you would recommend that they should NOT borrow more money. Quote TWO financial indicators with figures.

INFORMATION A — Financial indicators:
                                    28 Feb 2025   29 Feb 2024
Debt-equity ratio                    0.8 : 1        0.5 : 1
Return on average capital employed    8.2%          9.5%

INFORMATION B:
• Interest rate on loans: 12% p.a.
subQuestions.memoText:
TWO financial indicators (3 marks each: 1 indicator, 1 figures/trend, 1 explanation):

INDICATOR 1: Debt-equity ratio ✓
Figures/trend: INCREASED from 0.5 : 1 to 0.8 : 1 (by 0.3 : 1) ✓
Explanation: The financial RISK has increased / the company is already more reliant on debt to finance its operations — borrowing more will increase risk further. ✓

INDICATOR 2: % Return on average capital employed (ROTCE) ✓
Figures/trend: DECREASED from 9.5% to 8.2% (by 1.3 percentage points / by 13.7%) ✓
Explanation: The company is NEGATIVELY GEARED — the ROTCE (8.2%) is LOWER than the interest rate (12%). This means borrowed money is costing more than it is earning — taking on more debt would worsen this position. ✓

Teaching on negative gearing: When ROTCE < interest rate on loan, borrowing destroys value. The loan costs 12% but the company only generates 8.2% return on that capital.

subQuestions.label: 3.5 (Benefits of issuing shares)
subQuestions.questionText: The other option of financing the proposed expansions is to ISSUE MORE SHARES. Explain how this will benefit the company. Provide TWO points.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points ✓✓ ✓✓ (2 marks each; 1 mark for incomplete/partial response):

• The capital raised does NOT have to be REPAID to the shareholders (unlike a loan).
• The DEBT-EQUITY RATIO will IMPROVE (decrease), reducing financial risk.
• DIVIDENDS will only be declared if the company can AFFORD to do so — unlike loan repayments which are compulsory.
• NO INTEREST is paid on share capital — this will IMPROVE profits and cash flow.

subQuestions.questionText:
SHARE VALUE — Venus Ltd:

Explain why shareholders should NOT be satisfied with the share prices at the end of the financial year. Quote TWO relevant financial indicators and other related data.

INFORMATION A — Financial indicators:
                              28 Feb 2025   29 Feb 2024
Net asset value per share     1 025 cents   1 060 cents

INFORMATION B — Additional information:
                              28 Feb 2025   29 Feb 2024
Market price per share        1 000 cents   1 030 cents
subQuestions.memoText:
Financial indicators with figures and trends (2 marks each; 1 for indicator + figure, 1 for trend):

INDICATOR 1: Net asset value (NAV) per share DECREASED from 1 060 cents to 1 025 cents (by 35 cents / by 3.3%) ✓✓

INDICATOR 2: Market price per share DECREASED from 1 030 cents to 1 000 cents (by 30 cents / by 2.9%) ✓✓

FOR FULL 4 MARKS — must also include the comparison:
The MARKET PRICE per share (1 000 cents) is LOWER than the NAV per share (1 025 cents) — investors are paying less for shares than they are intrinsically worth. ✓

Teaching: Shareholders should ideally see:
(a) Rising NAV (growing book value per share).
(b) Rising market price.
(c) Market price ≥ NAV (shares trading at a premium or at least at book value).
All three have deteriorated — hence dissatisfaction.

subQuestions.label: 3.7 (Qualified CFO)
subQuestions.questionText:
RENEWAL OF CFO's CONTRACT — Venus Ltd:

Explain ONE reason why any company should appoint a SUITABLY QUALIFIED person as their chief financial officer (CFO).
subQuestions.memoText:
Any ONE valid point ✓✓ (2 marks for a well-explained point; 1 mark for incomplete/partial):

• To DEVELOP sound financial strategies aligned with the company's long-term goals.
• To ENSURE the company complies with financial regulations and standards (e.g. IFRS, Companies Act).
• To INSTIL CONFIDENCE in the company's performance and growth among investors and stakeholders.
• CFOs are instrumental in IDENTIFYING FINANCIAL RISKS before they become crises.
• Must have the RELEVANT KNOWLEDGE (experience/skills) as the CFO makes final decisions on all aspects of the company's finances.
• Must be informed of all POLICIES relevant to effective handling of the company's finances.
• To PREVENT FRAUD and mismanagement of funds.

subQuestions.label: 3.7 (Indicators for non-renewal)
subQuestions.questionText:
Apart from the factors and financial indicators covered in Questions 3.2 to 3.6, quote and explain TWO financial indicators why you feel that Denzel's contract should NOT be renewed.

INFORMATION A — Financial indicators (excluding those already discussed in 3.2–3.6):
                                        28 Feb 2025   29 Feb 2024
Earnings per share                      51 cents      58 cents
Return on average shareholders' equity   4.5%          6.2%
Solvency ratio                           2.2 : 1       2.6 : 1
% Operating expenses on sales            18.3%         22.7%

NOTE: Do NOT accept % operating expenses on sales. Do NOT repeat indicators used in 3.2–3.6.
subQuestions.memoText:
TWO financial indicators NOT used in 3.2–3.6 (2 marks each: 1 indicator + figures, 1 explanation/trend):

INDICATOR 1: Earnings per share (EPS) DECREASED from 58 cents to 51 cents (by 7 cents / by 12%) ✓
Explanation: Each share is EARNING LESS — the company is generating less profit per share under Denzel's financial management. ✓

INDICATOR 2: Return on average shareholders' equity DECREASED from 6.2% to 4.5% (by 1.7 percentage points / by 27.4%) ✓
Explanation: Shareholders are receiving a LOWER RETURN on their investment — the company is managing shareholders' funds less effectively. ✓

INDICATOR 3 (alternative): Solvency ratio DECREASED from 2.6 : 1 to 2.2 : 1 (by 0.4 : 1) ✓
Explanation: The company's long-term ability to cover ALL debts with ALL assets has DETERIORATED. ✓

NOTE: Do NOT accept % operating expenses on sales.
Be aware of relevant indicators NOT used in Q3.2–Q3.6 (exclude positive trends e.g. improved liquidity).

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to the audit report extract below. Identify the TYPE of audit report that Yungs Ltd received.

EXTRACT FROM AUDIT REPORT — VC Auditors to Yungs Ltd:

'Opinion: In our opinion the financial statements FAIRLY PRESENT, in all material respects, the financial position and cash flows of Yungs Ltd as at 28 February 2025. It was set in accordance with International Financial Reporting Standards (IFRS) and complied with the requirements of the Companies Act, 2008 (Act 71 of 2008) of South Africa.

Basis for Opinion: The audit evidence obtained is sufficient, reliable and appropriate to provide a basis for our opinion.'
subQuestions.memoText:
Unqualified report ✓
Also accept: 'clean' report

Teaching: Key phrases that identify an UNQUALIFIED report:
• 'Fairly present in all material respects'
• 'Sufficient, reliable and appropriate' evidence
• No exceptions, qualifications, or adverse opinions noted
An unqualified (clean) report is the BEST outcome — it means the auditors found the financial statements to be accurate and compliant.

subQuestions.questionText: Name TWO reliable types of audit evidence that VC Auditors used as the basis for their opinion on Yungs Ltd's financial statements.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid and different types of audit evidence ✓ ✓ (1 mark each):

• Source documents (e.g. invoices, receipts, delivery notes, credit notes)
• Journals (cash receipts journal, cash payments journal, etc.)
• Ledgers (general ledger, debtors ledger, creditors ledger)
• (Signed) Contracts
• (Signed) Payrolls
• Debtors' statements
• Creditors' statements
• Bank statements
• EFT vouchers / proof of payment
• Asset registers
• Physical inspections (e.g. physically counting inventory, inspecting fixed assets)
• Deeds / Registration documents

Be aware of other valid examples related to financial records.
Teaching: Reliable evidence is EXTERNAL (from outside the company) or involves physical verification. The most reliable evidence is obtained directly from third parties (e.g. bank statements, debtors' confirmations).

subQuestions.questionText: Explain how the UNQUALIFIED audit report received by Yungs Ltd could have a POSITIVE influence on the company in the future. Provide TWO points.
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points ✓✓ ✓✓ (2 marks each; 1 mark for incomplete/partial/unclear response):

• SHAREHOLDER CONFIDENCE: Shareholders will have confidence in the management of the company and would want to RETAIN their shares (reducing the risk of share sell-offs).
• ATTRACT INVESTORS: It would attract POTENTIAL SHAREHOLDERS / new investors.
• RAISING CAPITAL: It will make it easier (viable) for the company to RAISE MORE CAPITAL in the future.
• SECURING FINANCE: The company may find it easier to SECURE FINANCING from financial institutions / improved credit rating.
• TRUSTWORTHINESS: Reassures shareholders that the company's financials are trustworthy, reducing perceived risk.
• SHARE PRICE: It may INCREASE the share price of the company on the JSE.
subQuestions.topic: Corporate Governance - Impact of Audit Report

subQuestions.questionText:
Refer to the newspaper extract below. What action would Vintage Ltd have taken against the TWO DIRECTORS who appeared in court? Provide TWO points.

NEWSPAPER EXTRACT:
'An external independent auditor from VC Auditors, Josh Peters, was implicated in a corruption court case against two directors of Vintage Ltd. These directors allegedly paid bribe money to Josh to ensure that favourable reports were issued by VC Auditors on the performance of Vintage Ltd, although the company is close to bankruptcy.'
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points ✓✓ ✓✓ (2 marks each; 1 mark for incomplete/partial/unclear):

• SUSPENSION: They could have been SUSPENDED (with or without pay) while the investigations / court case are taking place.
• WITHHELD FEES: Directors' fees and/or directors' benefits may NOT have been paid out while the court case is taking place.
• DISMISSAL / DELINQUENCY: They could be DISMISSED or declared DELINQUENT directors if found guilty in court.
• REPAYMENT OF BRIBES: They may have been required to PAY BACK the bribe money to the company if found guilty.
• RECOVERY OF FEES: Vintage Ltd could CLAIM BACK any directors' fees or benefits earned during the period the offence occurred.

subQuestions.questionText: Explain TWO consequences that Josh Peters (the external auditor from VC Auditors) may face for his ILLEGAL conduct (accepting bribes to issue favourable audit reports).
subQuestions.memoText:
Any TWO valid points ✓✓ ✓✓ (2 marks each; 1 mark for incomplete/partial/unclear):

• DISCIPLINARY ACTION: Disciplinary action by his employer (VC Auditors) / lose his licence from his professional body (e.g. SAICA — South African Institute of Chartered Accountants).
• INVESTIGATION OF OTHER REPORTS: Other auditing reports he signed off may be investigated. He may lose credibility in his workplace and profession.
• EMPLOYER LEGAL ACTION: VC Auditors (employer) may SUE HIM for loss of future income / other auditing contracts due to their damaged reputation.
• CLIENT LEGAL ACTION: Vintage Ltd (client) could SUE HIM in his personal capacity to repay the total bribe money he received / he may lose his personal possessions.
• CRIMINAL PROSECUTION: If charged for fraud, he may face JAIL TIME / not be able to practise as an auditor in future.

Do NOT accept: 'Lose qualification'; 'blacklisted'; 'fired' (too vague — need specific consequences).
